Return the updated balance from both methods.
exercises.prompt:
Write a `BankAccount` class with:
- `__init__(self, owner, balance=0)` storing both as attributes
- `deposit(self, amount)` adding to balance and returning the new balance
- `withdraw(self, amount)` subtracting from balance (raise `ValueError` if amount > balance) and returning the new balance

Example:
```python
acct = BankAccount("amy", 100)
acct.deposit(50)    # -> 150
acct.withdraw(30)   # -> 120
acct.withdraw(500)  # raises ValueError
```

exercises.prompt:
Write a `@dataclass` called `Temperature` with a `celsius: float` field. Add a `fahrenheit` property that converts to Fahrenheit (`c * 9/5 + 32`), and validate in `__post_init__` that celsius is not below absolute zero (-273.15) — raise `ValueError` if it is.

Example:
```python

t.fahrenheit  # -> 212.0
Temperature(-300)  # raises ValueError
```

`__post_init__` runs automatically after the generated `__init__`.

lessons.body:
# Classes and __init__

A class bundles data (attributes) and behavior (methods). `__init__` is the constructor — it runs when you create an instance, and `self` refers to the instance being built.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name      # instance attributes, set per object
        self.age = age

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says woof!"

d = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(d.bark())    # Rex says woof!
print(d.name)      # Rex
```

`self` is explicit — Python has no implicit `this`. The first parameter of every instance method is the instance itself, and you must declare it. Forgetting `self` is the #1 beginner error and the fix is always the same: add it.

```python
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0        # every instance gets its own count

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

a, b = Counter(), Counter()
a.increment()
print(a.count, b.count)       # 1 0 — attributes live on the instance
```

Attributes don't need declaring up front — assigning `self.x` anywhere (usually `__init__`) creates it. This flexibility is powerful and also how you get `AttributeError` from typos, so keep `__init__` as the single place where attributes are born.
lessons.jsNote: Java: `__init__` is the constructor, `self` is `this` — except Python forces you to write `self` as a parameter instead of it being implicit. There are no access modifiers: everything is public, and privacy is by convention (single `_prefix`, double `__prefix` for name mangling — see the @property lesson). JavaScript: classes look similar on the surface (`constructor`, methods), but Python has no `new` keyword — `Dog(...)` calls the class directly.
keyPoints: `class` defines the blueprint; `__init__(self, ...)` initializes each instance.
`self` is explicit — always the first parameter of instance methods.
Attributes are created by assignment (`self.x = ...`), typically all in `__init__`.
Each instance gets its own attributes; nothing is shared unless you use class attributes.
lessons.title: Classes and __init__

lessons.body:
# Instance, class, and static methods

Most methods take `self` and operate on an instance. Two decorators give you the other flavors: `@classmethod` (takes the class) and `@staticmethod` (takes neither).

```python
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"   # class attribute: shared by ALL instances

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def bark(self):                          # instance method: needs self
        return f"{self.name} says woof!"

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data):                # class method: gets the class
        return cls(data["name"])             # alternative constructor

    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_name(name):                 # static: plain function in a namespace
        return isinstance(name, str) and len(name) > 0

d = Dog.from_dict({"name": "Rex"})   # call on the class, not an instance
print(Dog.species)                   # Canis familiaris
```

Class attributes (defined directly in the class body) are shared — one copy for the class and all instances. They're the right home for constants and defaults. But beware the mutable-class-attribute trap: a list defined as a class attribute is shared, so appending via one instance mutates it for all. When in doubt, initialize mutable state in `__init__`.

```python
class Team:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.members = []  # each team gets its OWN list — do this
```

Class methods shine as named alternative constructors (`from_dict`, `from_json`, `parse`) — a pattern you'll see constantly in real code. Static methods are rarer; they're just organizational — a function that logically belongs to the class but needs neither instance nor class state.
lessons.jsNote: Java: `@classmethod` is like a `static` factory method (`Dog.fromDict(...)`), except `cls` makes it inherit correctly in subclasses — Java statics don't do that. `@staticmethod` is a plain Java `static` method. Class attributes are `static` fields, including the exact same mutable-static-field trap Java developers already know to avoid. JavaScript: `static` methods in JS classes are closest to `@staticmethod`; Python has no direct equivalent of JS statics that need the class — that's `@classmethod`.
keyPoints: Instance methods take `self`; classmethods take `cls`; staticmethods take neither.
`@classmethod` is the idiom for alternative constructors (`from_dict`, `from_csv`).
Class attributes are shared across instances — never put mutable state there.
`@staticmethod` = namespaced helper function; use sparingly.
lessons.title: Instance, class, and static methods

lessons.jsNote: Java: `super().__init__(name)` is the `super(name)` constructor call — but in Python it's optional, and forgetting it just means parent state never initializes (no compiler error to save you). `ABC` + `@abstractmethod` are abstract classes/interfaces; the difference is Python checks at instantiation time, not compile time. There's no `implements` vs `extends` split and no method overloading by arity — same-name methods with different signatures just overwrite each other (use default arguments instead). JavaScript: `extends` / `super()` map directly; but JS has no abstract classes natively, and Python's duck typing is even more idiomatic than JS's.
keyPoints: `class Child(Parent):` inherits; `super().__init__(...)` runs the parent's constructor.
Override methods by redefining them; call the parent version via `super()`.
Duck typing is the default — formal interfaces via `abc.ABC` + `@abstractmethod` when you need enforcement.
Prefer shallow hierarchies and composition over deep inheritance.
lessons.title: Inheritance and super()

lessons.body:
# Dunder methods: making objects Pythonic

Methods wrapped in double underscores ("dunders") hook your class into Python's syntax. Define a few and your objects work with `print()`, `==`, `len()`, loops, and more.

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

    def __str__(self):                     # str(p), print(p), f"{p}"
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __repr__(self):                    # repr(p), debugger & logs
        return f"Point(x={self.x}, y={self.y})"

    def __eq__(self, other):                # p1 == p2
        return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)

p = Point(1, 2)
print(p)          # Point(1, 2)      <- __str__
print(repr(p))    # Point(x=1, y=2)  <- __repr__
```

`__str__` is for humans, `__repr__` is for developers — `__repr__` should ideally look like code that could recreate the object. If you define only one, make it `__repr__`: Python falls back to it when `__str__` is missing.

```python
class Playlist:
    def __init__(self):
        self.songs = []

    def add(self, song):
        self.songs.append(song)

    def __len__(self):                     # len(playlist)
        return len(self.songs)

    def __iter__(self):                    # for song in playlist
        return iter(self.songs)

pl = Playlist()
pl.add("Blue")
print(len(pl))          # 1
for s in pl:            # works because of __iter__
    print(s)
```

Important gotcha: defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to `None`, making your objects unhashable (unusable as dict keys or in sets) unless you also define `__hash__`. And default `==` without `__eq__` compares identity (`is`) — two objects with identical data are not equal unless you say so.
lessons.jsNote: Java: `__str__` = `toString()`, `__eq__` = `equals()` (and the `__hash__` gotcha is exactly the equals/hashCode contract — Java devs already know this pain), `__len__` / `__iter__` are like implementing `Iterable` / `size()`. One big difference: Python has no `.equals()` vs `==` split — `==` calls `__eq__`, while `is` is the identity check (Java's `==` on objects). JavaScript: the `==` vs `===` confusion doesn't exist here; Python's `==` is value equality via `__eq__`, always.
keyPoints: Dunders hook into syntax: `__str__`/`__repr__`, `__eq__`, `__len__`, `__iter__`.
`__repr__` is the developer-facing fallback — define it first.
Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` makes instances unhashable.
Default `==` is identity comparison; `__eq__` gives you value comparison.
lessons.title: Dunder methods: making objects Pythonic

lessons.jsNote: Java: `_balance` is package-private / `protected` by convention only — nothing stops access, so treat it as a team agreement. `@property` is a getter/setter pair that callers use as a field (`a.balance = 200` instead of `a.setBalance(200)`). `@dataclass` is Lombok's `@Data` or a Java `record` — auto-generated constructor, equals, and toString. JavaScript: `@property` is like JS getters/setters in classes (`get balance()`), which JS devs already use the same way.
keyPoints: Privacy is conventional: `_name` means internal; no compiler enforcement.
`@property` adds validation/computed attributes without changing the caller interface.
Don't write getters/setters preemptively — plain attributes first, property when needed.
`@dataclass` generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__` — ideal for data-holding classes.
lessons.title: @property and dataclasses
